title: Stuck Between Two Extremes
content:
Rethinking How Indians Share Their Identity

By: Abee Narayan | GitHub

Stuck Between Two Extremes

Identity verification today is trapped between two extremes: too little trust or too much disclosure.

Every day, millions of Indians are asked to prove their identity. Whether checking into a hotel, opening a bank account, verifying age on a social media platform, or collecting a parcel, the process usually follows one of two extremes. Either users simply self-declare information with no real verification, or they submit an entire government-issued identity document containing far more personal information than the service actually requires.

Consider online age verification. Most social media platforms simply ask users to tick a checkbox declaring they are above 18 years of age. The platform has no way of knowing whether that declaration is true, creating obvious concerns around child safety and age-inappropriate content.

The alternative is equally problematic. Asking users to upload their Aadhaar or another identity document exposes their full name, address, Aadhaar number, date of birth, and several other personal attributes when the platform only needs the answer to one question:

Is this person above the required age?

This illustrates a broader challenge in today's digital economy. Identity verification often requires people to share significantly more personal information than is necessary for the intended purpose.

The new Aadhaar App introduces a fundamentally different model—one where users share only the information required for a transaction while retaining complete control over their identity.

title: From Data Sharing to Verifiable Identity Claims
content:
From Data Sharing to Verifiable Identity Claims

At the heart of the new Aadhaar App is a simple but transformative principle: users should share only what is necessary, nothing more.

Rather than sharing physical documents or machine-readable identity records containing complete personal information, users share cryptographically verifiable proofs of specific claims.

Powered by Verifiable Credentials (VCs) and Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs), identity verification becomes purpose-specific and privacy-preserving. Instead of transmitting an entire identity record, the Aadhaar App responds only to the specific question being asked, revealing no additional information.

For example, a social media platform could generate a QR code or invoke the Aadhaar App using an app-to-app or web-to-app intent, requesting confirmation that a user meets the minimum age requirement. The user authenticates using a quick face verification within the Aadhaar App, which responds with a cryptographically verifiable "Yes" or "No.":

Is the user above 18? Yes.

Nothing more.

No Aadhaar number.

No date of birth.

No address.

No unnecessary personal information leaves the user's device.

The platform receives exactly what it needs to establish trust—no more, no less.

This represents a fundamental shift from full-disclosure identity verification to consent-driven, purpose-limited proof sharing, where users remain in control of their personal information while organizations receive only the information necessary to complete the transaction.

title: Building an Open Identity Ecosystem
content:
Building an Open Identity Ecosystem

Just as UPI created a common infrastructure that allowed banks and payment applications to interoperate seamlessly, the Aadhaar App adopts open standards that enable multiple wallets and verification applications to participate in a common digital identity ecosystem.

Rather than being tied to a single application, the ecosystem is designed around Verifiable Credentials (VCs), an internationally accepted standard for issuing, storing, and presenting digital identity credentials. Under this model, trusted organizations issue digitally signed credentials that users securely store in a digital wallet. Whenever proof of identity is required, users can selectively share only the information necessary for that transaction, while verifiers can independently confirm its authenticity using cryptographic verification.

Because the ecosystem is built on open standards, users are not restricted to the Aadhaar App alone. While the Aadhaar App serves as the native wallet, Aadhaar credentials can also be securely stored and presented through any compliant wallet, including global platforms such as Google Wallet. Likewise, businesses can accept identity proofs from any standards-compliant wallet without building separate integrations for each application.

This open architecture encourages innovation while preserving interoperability. Just as consumers today choose their preferred UPI application without worrying about compatibility, the Aadhaar Verifiable Credential ecosystem gives users the freedom to choose their preferred wallet while ensuring that every participant can interact through a common trust framework

title: What This Evolution Makes Possible
content:
What This Evolution Makes Possible

The emergence of this ecosystem reflects the broader evolution of India's Digital Public Infrastructure. Aadhaar was conceived at a time when smartphones were still uncommon, and identity verification was designed for the realities of that era. Today, smartphones have become the primary gateway through which citizens access digital services. Just as UPI transformed digital payments and DigiLocker transformed document exchange, the Aadhaar App extends trusted digital identity into a mobile-native experience.

This mobile-native approach is about much more than carrying Aadhaar on a smartphone. It fundamentally changes how trust is exchanged. Instead of sharing physical documents or complete digital identity records, individuals can now present cryptographically verifiable proofs that disclose only the information required for a specific purpose. While the underlying cryptography is sophisticated, its impact is remarkably simple: identity verification becomes more privacy-preserving, resilient, interoperable, and easier to adopt across the digital ecosystem.

title: Privacy by Design
content:
Privacy by Design

One of the most immediate outcomes of this new approach is the gradual transition away from India's long-standing dependence on photocopies of identity documents.

For decades, identity verification across sectors such as hospitality, the gig economy, visitor management, and numerous other service industries has relied on collecting photocopies of government-issued identity documents. Once submitted, these copies are often retained in filing cabinets, office computers, or enterprise databases, with little visibility for citizens into who can access them, how long they are retained, or how securely they are protected.

The Aadhaar App significantly reduces the need for this practice. Instead of collecting and storing complete identity documents, organisations receive cryptographically verifiable proofs tailored specifically to the transaction they are performing. They receive the assurance they need without becoming custodians of unnecessary personal information.

By embedding purpose limitation and data minimisation directly into the verification protocol, the Aadhaar App also makes it easier for organisations to align with the principles of India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act. Privacy is no longer an operational responsibility alone; it becomes a built-in property of the identity exchange itself.

title: Trust Beyond Connectivity
content:
Trust Beyond Connectivity

India's existing Aadhaar authentication ecosystem successfully processes approximately 80 million authentication transactions every day, providing trusted online identity verification at an unprecedented scale. However, certain environments continue to experience intermittent connectivity, making real-time verification challenging.

The Aadhaar App complements this architecture by securely shifting the trust anchor from the network to the user's own device. Instead of relying on connectivity during every transaction, trust is established during onboarding through hardware-backed device registration and cryptographic binding of the user's identity to that device.

Following successful face authentication, the Aadhaar credential is securely provisioned to the device as a Verifiable Credential. The credential can then be presented offline using QR codes, NFC, or Bluetooth, allowing verifiers to establish trust even in low-connectivity environments.

The result is an identity verification experience that is faster, more resilient, and capable of operating across both online and offline scenarios without compromising security.

title: Built for Easy Adoption
content:
Built for Easy Adoption

A privacy-preserving identity ecosystem can succeed only if organisations can integrate it without significant technical complexity.

To support a wide range of deployment scenarios, the Aadhaar App offers multiple integration options. Digital platforms can invoke the app directly through lightweight app-to-app and web-to-app integration flows, while physical verification scenarios such as service counters and kiosks can use standardised QR codes that initiate verification on the user's device. The architecture also supports proximity-based communication using NFC and Bluetooth where available.

Figure 4: Invocation methods

To further simplify implementation, UIDAI provides an open-source reference verifier codes that enables developers to rapidly build interoperable verification solutions without implementing complex identity infrastructure from scratch.

More importantly, these same standards extend beyond large technology platforms. Existing Point-of-Sale terminals, assisted-service devices, banking correspondent infrastructure, and third-party compliant wallets can all participate within the same ecosystem. This enables even small businesses and field operators to perform high-assurance identity verification using infrastructure they already possess.

Rather than storing sensitive identity databases and managing the associated regulatory obligations, organisations receive only the minimum cryptographic confirmation required for each transaction. This lowers implementation costs, reduces compliance burdens, and expands access to secure identity verification across the country.

title: Conclusion: Towards a Mobile-Native Trust Infrastructure
content:
Conclusion: Towards a Mobile-Native Trust Infrastructure

The Aadhaar App represents more than a new way of carrying Aadhaar on a smartphone. It represents the next stage in the evolution of India's Digital Public Infrastructure.

Over the past decade, India has transformed how money moves through UPI and how documents move through DigiLocker. The Aadhaar App extends this journey by transforming how trust moves across the digital economy.

Instead of repeatedly exchanging identity documents, individuals can now exchange trusted, cryptographically verifiable identity claims. Organisations receive only the information necessary to complete a transaction, while citizens remain in control of their personal information.

As more wallets, applications, and organisations adopt this open ecosystem, identity verification can become as seamless, interoperable, and privacy-preserving as digital payments are today.

For decades, small businesses and organisations outside formal KYC workflows have had few practical options beyond collecting copies of identity documents to establish trust. The Aadhaar App introduces a new model where organisations verify identity through cryptographically verifiable claims instead of storing sensitive personal information.

The future of digital trust will not be measured by how much information we share. It will be measured by how confidently we can establish trust while sharing only what is necessary.
